blocks.body:
A geometry problem usually arrives as a picture and a claim: three points are collinear, two lines are perpendicular, two lengths are equal. A synthetic proof needs the right auxiliary line or the right pair of similar triangles, and sometimes nobody finds one in time. Coordinates offer a different deal. Turn every point into numbers, turn the claim into an equation, and check the equation by algebra. No inspiration is needed, only patience.

The catch is that the same problem can take five lines in one frame and five pages in another. This lesson builds four frames (Cartesian coordinates, vectors, complex numbers and barycentric coordinates), proves the formulas each rests on, and discusses how to pick the one that keeps the computation short.

blocks.title: Cartesian coordinates and the choice of frame
blocks.body:
With $A=(x_1,y_1)$ and $B=(x_2,y_2)$, the distance is $AB=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}$, the midpoint is $\left(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\tfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$, and two lines with slopes $m_1,m_2$ are perpendicular exactly when $m_1m_2=-1$. The signed area of a triangle $P_1P_2P_3$ with $P_i=(x_i,y_i)$ is

$$[P_1P_2P_3]=\tfrac12\big((x_2-x_1)(y_3-y_1)-(x_3-x_1)(y_2-y_1)\big),$$

positive when the vertices run counterclockwise and zero exactly when the three points are collinear. So a collinearity claim becomes "this expression vanishes".

The work lies in placing the figure. A few rules that rarely fail: put the most important point at the origin; lay a line that carries many points along an axis; keep any symmetry (an isosceles triangle becomes $(-1,0),(1,0),(0,h)$); and scale one length to $1$. A general triangle can be taken as $B=(0,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $A=(u,v)$, which leaves only two free parameters. The cost of a coordinate proof grows quickly with the number of free parameters and with the degree of the expressions, so every symmetry kept in the frame pays for itself.

blocks.title: Vectors, with the circumcentre as origin
The orthocentre from the circumcentre
blocks.body:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcentre $O$ placed at the origin. Then its orthocentre $H$ has position vector

$$\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c.$$

Consequently $\mathbf h=3\mathbf g$: the points $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear (the Euler line) and $OH=3\,OG$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $H$ be the point with $\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$. Then

$$(\mathbf h-\mathbf a)\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=|\mathbf b|^2-|\mathbf c|^2=R^2-R^2=0.$$

So either $H=A$ or the line $AH$ is perpendicular to $BC$; in both cases $H$ lies on the altitude from $A$. The same computation with the letters permuted puts $H$ on the altitude from $B$. The altitudes from $A$ and $B$ are perpendicular to the non-parallel lines $BC$ and $CA$, so they are not parallel and meet in exactly one point, the orthocentre. Hence $H$ is the orthocentre. Finally $\mathbf g=\tfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=\tfrac13\mathbf h$, so $G$ lies on segment $OH$ with $OH=3\,OG$.

blocks.title: Complex numbers and the unit circle
Chords of the unit circle
Proof
blocks.body:
For $w=a-b$ we have $\bar w=\tfrac1a-\tfrac1b=\tfrac{b-a}{ab}$, so $w/\bar w=-ab$. Likewise $(c-d)/\overline{(c-d)}=-cd$. By the test above, the chords are parallel exactly when $-ab=-cd$ and perpendicular exactly when $-ab=cd$. This proves 2 and 3.

For 1: $z$ is on the line exactly when $z=a$ or $z-a$ is parallel to $b-a$, i.e. $\dfrac{z-a}{\bar z-\bar a}=-ab$. Clearing denominators, $z-a=-ab\,\bar z+ab\,\bar a=-ab\,\bar z+b$, which rearranges to $z+ab\,\bar z=a+b$. The point $z=a$ also satisfies this equation, since $a+ab\cdot\tfrac1a=a+b$. All steps reverse.

For 4: the foot $F$ lies on the line, so $F+ab\,\bar F=a+b$. Also $z-F$ is zero or perpendicular to $a-b$, which by the test means $z-F=ab\,(\bar z-\bar F)$, i.e. $F-ab\,\bar F=z-ab\,\bar z$. Adding the two equations gives $2F=a+b+z-ab\,\bar z$.

blocks.title: Barycentric coordinates
blocks.body:
Fix a reference triangle $ABC$. Every point $P$ of the plane can be written uniquely as $P=xA+yB+zC$ with $x+y+z=1$, where the combination is taken of position vectors (the result does not depend on the origin because the weights sum to $1$). The triple $(x,y,z)$ is the normalised barycentric coordinate of $P$; any nonzero multiple $(kx:ky:kz)$ names the same point in homogeneous form. In terms of signed areas,

$$x=\frac{[PBC]}{[ABC]},\qquad y=\frac{[APC]}{[ABC]},\qquad z=\frac{[ABP]}{[ABC]}.$$

The meaning: $P$ is the centre of mass of weights $x,y,z$ placed at the vertices.

blocks.title: Working in barycentrics
blocks.body:
Basic points look very clean in this frame: $A=(1:0:0)$; the midpoint of $BC$ is $(0:1:1)$; the centroid is $(1:1:1)$; the incentre is $(a:b:c)$ with $a,b,c$ the side lengths, because the triangles $IBC$, $ICA$, $IAB$ all have height $r$ and so have areas $\tfrac12ar$, $\tfrac12br$, $\tfrac12cr$. A point is on line $BC$ exactly when its first coordinate is $0$.

If $P=(u:v:w)$ with $v+w\ne0$, the line $AP$ meets $BC$ at $D=(0:v:w)$. Indeed $vB+wC=(u+v+w)P-uA$, so after dividing by $v+w$ the point $D=\tfrac{vB+wC}{v+w}$ is an affine combination of $A$ and $P$ (on line $AP$) and also of $B$ and $C$ (on line $BC$). From $D=\tfrac{vB+wC}{v+w}$ we read $BD:DC=w:v$. Doing the same at the other vertices, for $P$ inside the triangle

$$\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}\cdot\frac{AF}{FB}=\frac wv\cdot\frac uw\cdot\frac vu=1,$$

which is Ceva's theorem in one line. For areas there is a determinant formula: if $P_i=(x_i,y_i,z_i)$ are normalised, then $[P_1P_2P_3]=\det\begin{pmatrix}x_1&y_1&z_1\\x_2&y_2&z_2\\x_3&y_3&z_3\end{pmatrix}[ABC]$. In particular three points are collinear exactly when this determinant is $0$, and that test works with homogeneous coordinates too.

blocks.title: Choosing the frame
blocks.body:
No frame is best for everything. A rough guide:

- Many points on one circle, angle chasing, chords, rotations: complex numbers with that circle as the unit circle.
- Ratios along sides, cevians, areas, the centroid and incentre, concurrence: barycentrics.
- Right angles, distances, a visible axis of symmetry, conics: Cartesian coordinates with the axis on a coordinate line.
- Midpoints, parallelograms, centroids, sums of squared lengths: vectors, often with the circumcentre or centroid as origin.

Before computing, count the free parameters and the degree of what must be expanded; if either is high, try another origin or frame first.

blocks.title: The median length
blocks.body: In triangle $ABC$ let $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$, and let $m_a$ be the length of the median from $A$. Show that $4m_a^2=2b^2+2c^2-a^2$.
blocks.solution:
Take $A$ as origin, so $|\mathbf b|=c$ and $|\mathbf c|=b$. The midpoint of $BC$ is $\tfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$, so

$$4m_a^2=|\mathbf b+\mathbf c|^2=|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2+2\,\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c,\qquad a^2=|\mathbf b-\mathbf c|^2=|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2-2\,\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c.$$

Adding, $4m_a^2+a^2=2(b^2+c^2)$, which is the claim. Check with the $3$–$4$–$5$ right triangle, $a=5$, $b=4$, $c=3$: $4m_a^2=32+18-25=25$, so $m_a=\tfrac52$, half the hypotenuse, as it must be.

blocks.title: A ratio by barycentrics
blocks.body: In triangle $ABC$, the point $D$ on $BC$ satisfies $BD:DC=1:2$, and $E$ is the midpoint of $AD$. The line $BE$ meets $CA$ at $F$. Find $AF:FC$.
blocks.solution:
From $BD:DC=1:2$ we get $D=\tfrac23B+\tfrac13C$, so $D=(0,\tfrac23,\tfrac13)$. The midpoint of $AD$ is $E=\tfrac12A+\tfrac12D=(\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\tfrac16)$, or $(3:2:1)$ in homogeneous form.

By the rule proved above (applied at vertex $B$), the line $BE$ meets $CA$ at the point obtained by deleting the $B$-coordinate: $F=(3:0:1)$, i.e. $F=\tfrac34A+\tfrac14C$. So $F$ is one quarter of the way from $A$ to $C$, and $AF:FC=1:3$.

blocks.title: The nine-point circle
blocks.body: Let $O$ and $H$ be the circumcentre and orthocentre of triangle $ABC$, and $N$ the midpoint of $OH$. Prove that the three midpoints of the sides, the three midpoints of $AH$, $BH$, $CH$, and the three feet of the altitudes all lie on the circle with centre $N$ and radius $R/2$.
blocks.solution:
Put $O$ at the origin. By the theorem above $\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$, so $\mathbf n=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$.

Midpoint $M_a$ of $BC$: $\mathbf m_a-\mathbf n=\tfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)-\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=-\tfrac12\mathbf a$, of length $R/2$.

Midpoint $A'$ of $AH$: $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf h)-\mathbf n=\tfrac12(2\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)-\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=\tfrac12\mathbf a$, again of length $R/2$. The same holds at $B$ and $C$, so six of the points are on the circle. Moreover $M_a-N$ and $A'-N$ are opposite vectors, so $M_aA'$ is a diameter.

Foot $D$ of the altitude from $A$: $D$ lies on line $BC$, which passes through $M_a$, and on the altitude $AH$, which passes through $A'$, and these two lines are perpendicular. If $D$ differs from $M_a$ and $A'$, then $\angle M_aDA'=90^\circ$, so $D$ lies on the circle with diameter $M_aA'$, which is our circle. If $D$ coincides with $M_a$ or $A'$ it is on the circle anyway. The other two feet are handled the same way.

blocks.title: The Simson line
blocks.body: Let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, different from $A,B,C$, and let $X,Y,Z$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. Prove that $X,Y,Z$ are collinear (the Simson line).
blocks.solution:
Make the circumcircle the unit circle, so $\bar p=1/p$. By part 4 of the chord theorem,

$$x=\tfrac12\Big(b+c+p-\frac{bc}{p}\Big),\quad y=\tfrac12\Big(c+a+p-\frac{ca}{p}\Big),\quad z=\tfrac12\Big(a+b+p-\frac{ab}{p}\Big).$$

Subtracting and factoring,

$$x-y=\tfrac12\Big((b-a)-\frac cp(b-a)\Big)=\frac{(b-a)(p-c)}{2p},\qquad x-z=\frac{(c-a)(p-b)}{2p}.$$

Since $p\ne b$ and $c\ne a$, we have $x\ne z$, and the points are collinear exactly when

$$w=\frac{x-y}{x-z}=\frac{(b-a)(p-c)}{(c-a)(p-b)}$$

is real. Conjugate each factor using $\bar u=1/u$ on the circle: $\bar b-\bar a=\tfrac{a-b}{ab}$, $\bar p-\bar c=\tfrac{c-p}{pc}$, $\bar c-\bar a=\tfrac{a-c}{ac}$, $\bar p-\bar b=\tfrac{b-p}{pb}$. Then

$$\bar w=\frac{(a-b)(c-p)}{(a-c)(b-p)}\cdot\frac{ac\cdot pb}{ab\cdot pc}=\frac{(a-b)(c-p)}{(a-c)(b-p)}=w,$$

the last step changing two signs in the numerator and two in the denominator. So $w$ is real and $X,Y,Z$ are collinear.

blocks.body:
- $\bar z=1/z$ holds only for points on the unit circle. The orthocentre $h=a+b+c$ is usually not on it, and its conjugate is $\tfrac1a+\tfrac1b+\tfrac1c$, not $1/h$.
- Divisions hide hypotheses. Dividing by $p-b$ or by $v+w$ assumes points are distinct or a line is not parallel to a side; say so, and treat the excluded cases separately.
- Barycentric formulas such as the area determinant need normalised coordinates (sum $1$); homogeneous coordinates must be divided by their sum first, except in tests of the form "determinant $=0$".
- Signed areas change sign with orientation. Mixing signed and unsigned areas is the most common source of wrong signs.

The methods rest on [[euclid-basics]] and on the algebra of [[complex-numbers]] and [[vectors-plane]]. Complex coordinates make the maps of [[geo-transformations]] explicit: a spiral similarity is $z\mapsto\alpha z+\beta$, and inversion in the unit circle is $z\mapsto1/\bar z$. The classical centres and lines of [[triangle-centres]] (Euler line, nine-point circle, Simson line) are natural test cases, and problems from [[circles]] often become one-line identities on the unit circle. The area formulas are determinants, see [[determinants]], and symmetric expressions in $a,b,c$ are handled with [[polynomials-roots|Vieta's formulas]]. Inequalities can be proved in the same frames: the identity $(a-b)(c-d)+(a-d)(b-c)=(a-c)(b-d)$, valid for any complex numbers, together with the triangle inequality for $|\cdot|$, gives Ptolemy's inequality $AB\cdot CD+AD\cdot BC\ge AC\cdot BD$, a starting point for [[geo-inequalities]].

1. With $a,b$ on the unit circle, show that the reflection of a point $z$ in the line $ab$ is $a+b-ab\,\bar z$.
2. With the circumcentre at the origin, prove that $OH^2=9R^2-(a^2+b^2+c^2)$, where $a,b,c$ are the side lengths.
3. In barycentric coordinates, let $D=(0:1:1)$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Find the point dividing $AD$ in the ratio $2:1$ from $A$, and confirm that it is $(1:1:1)$.
4. Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular and meet at $P$. Using the unit circle and $ac+bd=0$, prove that the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$ passes through the midpoint of $CD$.
